query: For W–Cu metal-matrix composites used in heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications, what single intervention could increase thermal conductivity while retaining mechanical durability and irradiation resistance? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite, defines the application conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a functionally graded W–Cu metal-matrix composite, with increased Cu content in the high-heat-flux regions and higher W content in the structural regions, will increase overall thermal conductivity while preserving mechanical durability and irradiation resistance compared to a uniform W–Cu composite.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogeneous W–Cu composite designed for operation in fusion reactor components (e.g., divertor), subjected to high heat flux and neutron irradiation.
generation.intervention: Use a tailored W–Cu composition gradient (functionally graded design) produced via layered/gradient powder metallurgy or controlled infiltration processes.
generation.conditions: High thermal flux and neutron irradiation conditions typical of the plasma-facing and heat-sink regions in fusion reactors.
generation.structural_mediator: A gradual transition from copper-rich zones (to enhance heat conduction) to tungsten-rich zones (for mechanical and irradiation resilience).
generation.mechanism: A localized increase in Cu content at the heat-loaded surface lowers thermal boundary resistance and boosts heat transfer, while the tungsten-enriched region maintains mechanical robustness and neutron damage tolerance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under fusion-reactor thermal and irradiation conditions, the functionally graded W–Cu composite will exhibit notably higher effective thermal conductivity and retain mechanical strength and irradiation resistance on par with or better than a uniform W–Cu composite baseline.
generation.baseline: A uniform W–Cu composite with a fixed ratio of copper and tungsten throughout its thickness.
generation.boundary: If the compositional gradient is not carefully optimized, thermal stresses or microstructural instabilities could lead to inferior mechanical or irradiation performance, limiting overall gains.
generation.uncertainty: Exact improvements in thermal conductivity and mechanical properties depend on the gradients’ profile and microstructural control, thus requiring empirical optimization for specific reactor conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Manufacture two sets of samples: a standard (uniform) W–Cu composite and a composition-graded W–Cu composite via layered infiltration or powder metallurgy. Expose both sets to elevated thermal flux and simulated neutron irradiation conditions representative of reactor environments.
measurements: Finite element modeling of temperature distribution across the graded layer
Microstructural analysis (SEM/TEM) before and after irradiation
Mechanical properties (hardness, tensile strength) before and after irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the functionally graded composite does not exhibit higher thermal conductivity than the uniform composite or if its mechanical/irradiation performance degrades more significantly under the same conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this context, one of the biggest challenges is the development of structural and functional materials that can withstand the conditions inside the reactor: high temperature, high heat flux, and intense flux of high energy neutrons []. The diverter, located at the bottom of the plasma chamber, where the thermal power from the plasma is exhausted [], is one of the most challenging areas. Tungsten (W), with a high melting temperature, low sputtering rates, low neutron activation, and low tritium and deuterium retention [,], was chosen as the plasma-facing material. CuCrZr alloy was chosen as the heat sink due to its high thermal conductivity and strength. However, there is a gap between the operating temperatures of these two materials. Tungsten presents a high ductile–brittle temperature transition (DBTT) [], which requires a high-temperature operation, while CuCrZr alloy presents relatively low working temperatures (180–350 °C) [], with loss of ductility caused by irradiation embrittlement at lower temperatures and loss of mechanical strength at higher temperatures due to over-aging [,]. Nuclear fusion-based power reactors require advancements with regard to high-temperature and plasma-facing materials in order to prevent degradation due to the exposure to high-temperature and high-energy neutron flux produced during deuterium-tritium fusion reactions. The severity of the service environment is expected to increase in upcoming fusion reactors with increased power ratings and those under transient scenarios. For instance, the heat load on the divertor, a key component of the tokamak design, , is expected to increase to 10 MW/m2 (steady state) and 20 MW/m2 (transient for 10 seconds). The inner and outer vertical targets of the divertor, where the kinetic energy of plasma particles is converted into heat, must withstand loads up to ~7–40 MJ/m2 and ~4–25 MJ/m2, respectively, under plasma disruption, . Therefore, unprecedented thermal, mechanical and physical characteristics are required for fusion reactor materials.

While pure W may have the most ideal combination of the He bubble size and density of the materials studied here, there are significant concerns for the usage of W in a fission or fusion reactor, including its ductile–brittle transition temperature, recrystallization, and the ability to fabricate complex components. The performance of additively manufactured RHEAs in other areas relevant for reactors, including fracture properties and recrystallization performance, must be explored further. Future studies will elucidate the mechanical performance and high-temperature performance of the RHEAs studied here, including the potential for self-healing. Helium irradiation and He bubble formation and accumulation is just one aspect of materials design that should motivate materials choices for future reactors. In this work, we show that compositionally complex (spanning two, three, and four-component alloys) can be developed with AM processing routes.
